claims.overstatement: Minor: 'none' rests on Table 2's 0%, printed to whole percent; with 347 cases one death (0.29%) would also print as 0%, so the table shows at most one such death, not necessarily none. Suggest 'Table 2 gives 0%'. Otherwise exact: 347 cases, median 0.002 mg/L (= 2 ng/mL), 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L.
claims.note: The 347 include findings below the 0.001 mg/L quantification limit counted as positive; the median and percentiles use quantified values only. The THC median lies below the compiled plasma reference range (relationship 0.40), consistent with the claim's caution that whole-blood post-mortem THC is hard to compare with plasma values. Femoral blood was taken at autopsy, on average five days after death.

anchors.extracted: THC in femoral blood in 347 cases; LOQ 0.001 mg/L; mean 0.005, median 0.002 mg/L; 90th 0.008, 95th 0.013, 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L; therapeutic plasma range 0.005-0.01 mg/L; fatal poisonings with THC as the main finding 0%; PM blood/plasma relationship 0.40.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Data refining, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 57,903 autopsy cases with comprehensive post-mortem drug analysis, 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2010; drugs detected at least 50 times; findings below LOQ included as positive; medians and percentiles from quantified values; share of deaths certified as fatal poisonings with that drug as the main finding, from the forensic pathologists' death certificates (ICD-10 plus ATC code).

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Toxicological analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Police inquest into sudden or unexpected deaths; medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist, who decides on toxicology; one national laboratory (>6,500 cases a year, >13% of deaths); femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, on average 5 days after death; results sent to the pathologist before the death certificate is issued.

claims.overstatement: None material. 'Sampled on average five days after death' = mean interval from death to autopsy, when femoral blood was taken. 'By up to 100-fold' rests on one drug, hydroxychloroquine, whose plasma range is printed as '-0.1' mg/L; the next largest ratios are 24 (promazine) and 16 (levomepromazine). 'Certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings by that drug' = fatal poisonings with that drug as the main finding. In the magnitude, 35.7% is the exact share (46/129); the paper prints 35%.
claims.note: Recomputed from Table 2 in my tab: printed relationships 61 = 1, 46 > 1, 22 < 1 (sum 129) confirmed. Applying the stated rule with single-value reference ranges treated as points gives 58 within, 48 above and 23 below, the same as the card's editors' calculation: aminophenazone (reference 10, median 15, ratio 1.5), tizanidine (about 0.015, median 0.02, 1.33) and risperidone (about 0.006, median 0.004, 0.67) are printed as 1, whereas dixyrazine and ketoprofen, also single values, are printed below 1. Printed ratios that depart from the rule without changing category: desmethyldiazepam 0.13 (rule 0.50, divided by the upper limit), metformin 5.5 (6.0), phenazepam 2.1 (2.25), betaxolol 1.9 (2.0), amlodipine 4.5 (4.67). The Conclusions print 59,903 cases for 57,903; Table 1's men and women sum to 57,886. The claim's last sentence (certifiers knew the levels) holds here: results went to the forensic pathologist before certification; the authors' remark that pathologists lacked the published distributions does not change that.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: A sudden or unexpected death leads to a police inquest; the police launch a medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist if needed (always when the death is not known to be due to disease or is linked to accident, crime, suicide, poisoning and similar); about 50,000 deaths and 11,000 medico-legal autopsies a year; toxicology samples taken on the forensic pathologist's decision; one laboratory analyses >6,500 cases a year, over 13% of all deaths.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Toxicological analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Interval from death to autopsy on average five days, bodies in cold storage at 3-5 °C; femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, preserved with 1% NaF, analysis mostly completed within 12 days.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Data refining, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: 57,903 autopsy cases with comprehensive drug analysis, 2000-2010; 129 drugs detected at least 50 times; medians from quantified values only (findings below LOQ left out); fatal-poisoning share from death certificates (drug as the main finding); relationship = 1 if the median lies within the plasma therapeutic range (Schulz et al., 2012), median/lower limit if below, median/upper limit if above.

anchors.locator: Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
anchors.extracted: 61 drugs (47%) had a relationship of 1, 22 (17%) below 1 and 46 (35%; exactly 35.7%) above 1; 36 drugs had more than 10% of cases certified as fatal poisonings with that drug as the main finding.

Buprenorphine 671 cases, median 0.0012 mg/L, therapeutic 0.0005-0.005, fatal poisonings 45%, relationship 1; methadone 207, 0.40 mg/L, 0.1-0.5, 43%, 1; morphine 1094, 0.07 mg/L, 0.01-0.1, 4%, 1; hydroxychloroquine 165, 10 mg/L, range printed '-0.1', 14%, relationship 100 (highest; next promazine 24).

For strong opioids used non-medically, such as buprenorphine and methadone, the post-mortem concentration plays a somewhat limited role in assessing the cause of death (authors' earlier studies, refs 30-31); partly also for amphetamine and other drugs where tolerance becomes important.

Fatal drug poisonings are about 8% and all fatal poisonings about 15% of toxicologically investigated cases, so medians mostly reflect normal post-mortem levels, but for the 36 drugs with more than 10% poisonings the normal level is probably below the median; pathologists did not have these distributions when certifying.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Analysis results are sent to the forensic pathologist, who later issues the death certificate with cause and manner of death, so the certifier knew the case's measured concentrations.

Amlodipine 0.07 mg/L in a driver killed in a crash would look like serious intoxication against clinical plasma values (therapeutic 0.003-0.015, toxic from 0.088 mg/L) yet is the post-mortem median of 313 cases; the authors conclude that judging post-mortem results by clinical plasma ranges would commonly misjudge a normal post-mortem level as lethal.

Plasma reference values are often applied carelessly to post-mortem whole blood; blood/plasma ratios differ more than twofold for some drugs. Relationships above 1 were common for basic drugs, thought largely due to post-mortem redistribution (antidepressants 1.2-4.7, antipsychotics 1.8-24); extensively plasma-bound drugs had lower post-mortem blood levels.

claims.overstatement: Minor: 'certified none of them as MDMA poisoning' should read 'none as a fatal poisoning with MDMA as the main finding'; a poisoning attributed mainly to another drug, with MDMA contributing, is not excluded. With 57 cases, 0% does mean no such death (one would print as 2%).
claims.note: The MDMA median (0.30 mg/L) lies within the compiled plasma reference range the authors used (0.1-0.35 mg/L, from Schulz et al., 2012), which is not a measurement in this study; consistent with the claim's closing statement that no study measured MDMA after ordinary use. N includes findings below the 0.04 mg/L LOQ; percentiles use quantified values.

anchors.extracted: MDMA in femoral blood in 57 cases; LOQ 0.04 mg/L; mean 0.76, median 0.30 mg/L; 90th 2.1, 95th 3.5, 97.5th percentile 4.0 mg/L; therapeutic plasma range 0.1-0.35 mg/L; fatal poisonings with MDMA as the main finding 0%; relationship 1.
